result.area_summary: Document-type taxonomies missing from the report's section 1.3 artifact-schema survey. The existing survey (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289, RUP artifacts, Scrum commitments, Prompty, MCP resources) covers what an artifact must contain but omits the two mature traditions that govern how artifact KINDS themselves are derived and bounded: DITA 1.3 (OASIS standard, 17 Dec 2015), whose information typing gives a small closed set of base topic types sharing one structural envelope and whose specialization architecture is a formally governed mechanism for deriving new constrained types from generic types with declared ancestry and guaranteed fallback processing — the strongest external anchor found for the shop's need to derive new artifact kinds from generic types; and Diátaxis (Procida, diataxis.fr), which classifies documents on an orthogonal axis to 15289 — by user need (acquisition/application x action/cognition) rather than content genre — and contributes the directly lintable rule that a document serves exactly one type. arc42 (verified, context-only) shows the fixed-numbered-skeleton-with-tailoring pattern for a single composite artifact kind; docs-as-code (Write the Docs; Gentle's Docs Like Code) is the verified name of the toolchain substrate the shop already runs on. All sources confirmed against primary pages; the diataxis.fr homepage summary misattributed authorship (Tom Christie), corrected against the colophon page which names Daniele Procida — a caution for anyone re-verifying via summary fetches. Net integration for section 2.3: 15289 remains the content anchor; DITA specialization becomes the derivation anchor; Diátaxis becomes the audience-need axis each kind declares; docs-as-code names the enforcement substrate.

findings.name: DITA 1.3 information typing and maps
findings.tradition: Technical communication / structured authoring (OASIS standardization of IBM's Darwin Information Typing Architecture)
findings.citation: OASIS Standard, Darwin Information Typing Architecture (DITA) Version 1.3, 17 December 2015 (Errata 02, 2018); Part 3 architectural spec sections "DITA terminology and notation", "Information typing", and "DITA maps". Information typing traces its lineage to Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique.
findings.what_it_defines: Typed topics as the unit of authoring: every topic is one of a small set of information types — base triad concept/task/reference, extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting — each a specialization of a single generic <topic> type sharing one structural envelope (title + prolog metadata + body). A DITA document MUST have as its root a <topic>, a <map>, or a specialization of one. Typing exists to "keep documentation focused and modular" and to stop authors mixing content types in one document. Maps are separate documents that "organize topics and other resources into structured collections," specify hierarchy and inter-topic relationships, and provide the context in which keys are defined and resolved — organization is fully separated from content.
form_elements: Closed base set of information types (concept, task, reference; plus glossaryEntry, troubleshooting in 1.3), each with a distinct purpose and content constraint
Uniform structural envelope across all types: title + prolog (metadata) + body
Task type as the procedure shape: enumerated steps toward one intended outcome
Normative root-element rule: document root MUST be <topic>/<map> or a specialization thereof
Maps as a separate artifact kind that assembles typed topics into deliverables and carries relationships and key-resolution context
Stated anti-pattern: mixing information types within one topic
findings.fit_notes: Maps directly onto the report's 2.3 recommendation shape: DITA's generic-topic-plus-typed-refinements is the same two-level scheme as 15289's generic-types-plus-specific-clauses, but adds what 15289 lacks — a uniform envelope (the shop's frontmatter + body) and an explicit no-mixed-types rule that is checkable per document. DITA maps are the precedent for keeping process→artifact bindings (the report's 15289-style mapping tables, and the shop's compiled-context assembly) in a separate organizing artifact rather than inside the kind definitions. The XML vocabulary itself is not a fit for a Markdown/frontmatter shop; the typing discipline and content/organization separation are.

findings.name: DITA 1.3 specialization architecture
findings.citation: OASIS Standard, DITA Version 1.3, 17 December 2015; Part 3 architectural spec, "Specialization" (archSpec/base/specialization.html) and "DITA terminology and notation".
findings.what_it_defines: A governed mechanism for deriving new document/element types from existing ones: specialization is "defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types," allowing architects to "define new kinds of information... while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible." Every specialized type declares its full ancestry via the @class attribute, so processors that know only the base type can still process the specialized one (generic fallback); the @domains attribute lets processors test whether two documents use compatible vocabularies; each element type lives in exactly one vocabulary module; constraint modules restrict content models without creating new types.
form_elements: Derivation-by-refinement: a new type is always a semantic refinement of an existing type, never invented from nothing
Declared ancestry chain (@class) carried by every instance, enabling both specialization-aware processing and graceful fallback to the base type
Compatibility declaration (@domains) making it decidable whether two documents share a vocabulary
One-vocabulary-module-per-type modularization rule
Constraint modules: governed restriction of an existing type's content model as a distinct, lighter operation than creating a new type
Design goal stated as reuse of existing design and processing across all derived types
findings.fit_notes: This is the external anchor the shop's kind-derivation mechanism lacks and the task asked to be evaluated. The report's 2.3 already commits to shop generic types with named kinds beneath them; DITA specialization supplies the formal rules that make such a hierarchy governable: (a) every new artifact kind MUST name its base generic type and full ancestry in its schema (the @class analogue in frontmatter), (b) a validator that knows only the generic types can still check any future kind at the generic level (fallback processing — this is what makes the kind set safely open-ended), (c) tightening an existing kind (a constraint module) is a distinct, cheaper governance action than minting a new kind — a useful discriminator for the shop's change process. Adopt the derivation rules; reject the XML/DTD machinery.

findings.name: Diátaxis
findings.tradition: Software documentation practice (originated in Procida's work at Divio, 2014–2021; widely adopted, e.g. hundreds of documentation projects per the site)
findings.citation: Daniele Procida, Diátaxis: A systematic approach to technical documentation authoring, diataxis.fr (author and origins confirmed on the site's colophon page; CITATION.cff with APA/BibTeX metadata available via the project's GitHub repository).
findings.what_it_defines: Four documentation types — tutorials, how-to guides, (technical) reference, explanation — generated as the quadrants of two axes of user need: action/cognition ("a skill or craft... contains both action (practical knowledge, knowing how...) and cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that...)") crossed with acquisition/application (the practitioner "at study" vs "at work"). Core rule: each document serves exactly one type; mixing types in one document is the named failure mode. The type determines all three of "documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)".
form_elements: 2x2 generative matrix: action/cognition x acquisition/application yields exactly four types

Tutorial = acquisition+action (learning by doing, author-led); how-to = application+action (task at work, user-led); reference = application+cognition (propositional, at work); explanation = acquisition+cognition (understanding, at study)
One-type-per-document rule as the central structural constraint
Type entails content, style, and architecture — a single classification drives three families of derived checks
Classification by the reader's moment of need, not by content genre
findings.fit_notes: Contributes the axis 15289 does not have: 15289 classifies by content genre (description/plan/report...), Diátaxis by user need at moment of use. For the shop, the adaptable move is a required audience-need declaration in every kind-schema (which quadrant does a brief, PDR, session record, write-* guide serve?) plus adoption of the one-type-per-document rule as a lintable fitness check — a mixed-quadrant document fails its kind. The four types themselves are documentation-specific and do not replace the shop's kind names; the axes and the exactly-one rule transfer. Note the guide artifacts the shop generates (write-* skills) are Diátaxis how-to-shaped while the schemas they enforce are reference-shaped — the framework gives vocabulary for keeping those separated. Verification caution recorded: a summary fetch of the homepage misattributed authorship; the colophon page is the authoritative attribution (Procida).

findings.name: arc42
findings.tradition: Software architecture documentation (German-origin, English-standard template; in practice since 2005)
findings.citation: Peter Hruschka and Gernot Starke, arc42 — Template for architecture communication and documentation, arc42.org (overview page; open source, free including commercial use).
findings.what_it_defines: A single fixed 12-section template for one composite artifact kind (the architecture description): 1 Introduction & Goals, 2 Constraints, 3 Context & Scope, 4 Solution Strategy, 5 Building Block View, 6 Runtime View, 7 Deployment View, 8 Crosscutting Concepts, 9 Architectural Decisions, 10 Quality Requirements, 11 Risks & Technical Debt, 12 Glossary — grouped as Requirements & Quality / Structures & Views / Concepts, Technologies & Decisions. Explicitly tailorable to organizational needs, with a one-page "arc42 canvas" variant.
form_elements: Fixed numbered section skeleton (12 sections) whose numbering is stable across uses
Three-part grouping of sections by concern
Embedded slot for decision records (section 9) inside a larger composite artifact — composition rather than replacement of the ADR kind
Explicit tailoring permission plus a canonical lightweight variant (canvas)
Answers both what to document and how, in one template
findings.fit_notes: Context-only for the report: it is a template for one artifact kind, not a taxonomy of kinds, and the shop's decision/product records (ADR, PDR) plus 15289 generic types already cover its territory. Two precedents worth citing in passing in 2.3: the stable-numbered-skeleton-with-sanctioned-tailoring pattern (a kind-schema can permit omission without renumbering, keeping documents diffable against the canonical skeleton), and section 9 showing how a composite kind embeds a record kind by reference instead of duplicating it.

findings.name: Docs as code
findings.tradition: Software documentation practice (Write the Docs community; corporate practice at Google, Microsoft, AWS, Twitter, Rackspace per conference record)
findings.citation: Write the Docs, "Docs as Code", writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/; canonical book-length treatment: Anne Gentle, Docs Like Code: Collaborate and Automate to Improve Technical Documentation (referenced on that page, alongside Etter's Modern Technical Writing and Lakatos's Crafting Docs for Success).
findings.what_it_defines: The philosophy that "you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code": documentation lives in plain-text markup (Markdown, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc) under version control (Git), with issue trackers, code review of doc changes, and automated tests in CI. Stated outcome is "a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation." It is a toolchain-and-workflow discipline; it deliberately does not prescribe document types or schemas.
form_elements: Plain-text markup as the storage format
Version control (Git) and issue tracking as the system of record for docs
Peer review of documentation via the code-review mechanism
Automated tests / CI gates on documentation
Shared writer-developer ownership as the cultural goal
findings.fit_notes: Adopt, and mostly already adopted de facto: the shop's Markdown artifacts in git, bead-tracked, reviewed, and schema-validated ARE docs-as-code — citing the practice in the report names and legitimizes the substrate on which every other recommendation (BCP 14 linting, frontmatter validation, Diátaxis-rule checks, hash-pinned scenarios) becomes mechanically enforceable in CI. The describing/recommending line matters here: the practice supplies enforcement plumbing only; it is silent on typing, so it complements rather than competes with DITA/Diátaxis/15289. Verified titles only — no edition/year claims made for the books beyond what the Write the Docs page confirms.

result.area_summary: Role-responsibility ASSIGNMENT formats — the gap in the report's §1.2, which covers role DEFINITION containers (SPEM, RUP, Scrum, subagent files) but not the cross-cutting forms that assign responsibilities across roles per deliverable or decision. Three traditions were surveyed and verified. (1) The project-management responsibility matrix line: the RAM/RACI chart as carried in the PMBOK Guide (PMI's authoritative treatment; glossary definitions confirmed verbatim), descending from the 1960s Linear Responsibility Chart (Cleland & King 1968); its load-bearing one-Accountable-per-row rule; its letter-set variants (RASCI/RACI-VS/CAIRO etc., inventoried on the Wikipedia RAM page); and its decision-rights fork — Bain's RAPID (Rogers & Blenko, HBR Jan 2006, primary-verified) and Atlassian/Intuit's DACI — which re-target the matrix from tasks to decisions with a single-Decider rule. Recurrent practitioner failure modes: multiple As dissolving accountability, R/A conflation, team-level (unnamed-individual) assignments, consulted-list bloat, and shelfware/illusion-of-clarity. (2) Holacracy's constitutionalized role anatomy (Constitution v5.0, §1.1: name + Purpose + Domains + Accountabilities-as-gerunds), its strict role-vs-person separation (§1.2/1.4.1), and its governance-meeting amendment protocol (Art. 5: tension-driven proposals, integrative decision-making, four-criteria objection testing) — the strongest external match for change-controlled, person-independent role definitions, with a documented failure exemplar (Medium's 2016 exit: over-codification taxed proactivity). (3) Team Topologies' three interaction modes (collaboration / X-as-a-Service / facilitating) as a typed vocabulary for role-to-role relationships, which nothing in the current survey provides. Fit anchor throughout: the system already enforces the one-A analog via RUP's one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule (report §2.2), so a RACI adds the C/I dimension that rule lacks — directly serviceable for the pending PO-vs-Architect RACI investigation. Section 1 material describes; adopt/adapt calls below are recommendations for section 2 and remain the product authority's to ratify.

findings.name: RACI responsibility-assignment matrix (RAM)
findings.citation: PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), 6th ed., 2017 — Plan Resource Management (§9.1) data-representation tools and glossary: RAM = "a grid that shows the project resources assigned to each work package"; RACI chart = "a common type of RAM that uses responsible, accountable, consult, and inform statuses to define the involvement of stakeholders in project activities" (definitions confirmed via PMI-affiliated PMP literature quoting the Guide; RAM treatment sits at p. 262 in the 5th ed.). Ancestry: the Linear Responsibility Chart in Cleland & King, Systems Analysis and Project Management, McGraw-Hill, 1968 (see also PMI Library, "Early Literature of Modern Project Management", pmi.org/learning/library/early-literature-modern-project-management-3542). The R-A-C-I lettering itself has no documented single originator — the Wikipedia RAM article and PMI-adjacent literature carry no dated origin; folklore attributions (GE, 1950s) are unverified and should not be cited.
findings.what_it_defines: A two-dimensional matrix crossing work items (rows: tasks, work packages, or deliverables) with roles (columns), each cell holding one involvement status: Responsible (does the work), Accountable (the one ultimately answerable for correct completion), Consulted (two-way input sought before/while), Informed (one-way notification after). The one-A rule — exactly one Accountable per row — is the form's load-bearing constraint; evidence status: the PMBOK glossary defines only the four statuses, while the one-A rule is stated as hard doctrine throughout PMI-affiliated exam/practitioner literature and is echoed at decision granularity by Bain's single-Decider rule (RAPID). Recurrent documented failure modes from practitioner criticism: (a) multiple As on one row dissolve accountability; (b) R/A conflation — the doer assumes they also judge sufficiency, removing oversight; (c) assigning R/A to a team rather than a named role/individual, so no one is individually answerable; (d) Consulted-list bloat slowing work; (e) shelfware — the chart is drafted once, never consulted, producing an illusion of clarity (e.g., tallyfy.com/raci-matrix and similar critiques; secondary sources, cited as criticism-in-circulation, not authority).
form_elements: Rows: deliverables / work packages / tasks (the unit of assignment is the work item, not the role)
Columns: roles (positions, not persons)
Cell vocabulary: R / A / C / I with defined semantics (R = completes the work; A = solely answerable for correct completion; C = two-way consultation; I = one-way notification)
One-A-per-row rule: exactly one Accountable for each deliverable
Audit rules implied by the form: no empty rows, no row with zero or multiple As, flag rows with many Cs, every R/A a named role
findings.fit_notes: The system already enforces the one-A analog: report §2.2 adopts RUP's one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule, which is exactly a standing A column over artifact kinds. What RACI adds that the RUP rule lacks is the C/I dimension — precisely what the pending PO-vs-Architect RACI investigation needs: rows = artifact kinds and decision points (brief, PDR, scenario set, dispatch, clarify response, reconciliation), columns = lead-po, lead-architect, router, BC; the A column must reproduce the existing artifact→role bindings (a consistency check, not a new decision), while C and I capture what is currently only implicit in clarify-routing and Monitor-event rules (who is Consulted on a scope clarify, who is Informed of a work_done). Failure modes map directly: multiple-A = the ambiguous-clarify-routing problem the router rules already wrestle with; shelfware risk is structurally low here because definitions compile into agent context rather than living in a drawer — but only if the matrix is derived into role frontmatter/primers, not kept as a standalone page. Format note: the matrix is an assignment overlay across role definitions, not a role-definition container — it complements, not replaces, the §2.2 subagent-file form.

findings.name: RASCI and the RACI letter-set variant family
findings.citation: Variant inventory as carried on the Wikipedia RAM article (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsibility_assignment_matrix): RASCI/RACIS/RASIC/RASI (adds S = Support), RACIQ (Q = Quality review), RACIO/CAIRO (O = Omitted / out-of-the-loop), RACI-VS(L) (V = Verifier, S = Signatory), PARIS (Participant / Accountable / Review required / Input required / Sign-off required), RACI+F (Facilitation). No variant has a single authoritative standard; all are practitioner extensions of the PMBOK-carried base form.
findings.what_it_defines: Letter-set extensions to the base RACI cell vocabulary, each adding a distinguished involvement status while preserving the matrix form and (in every variant) the one-A rule. The most adopted is RASCI: S = Support, a role that assists the Responsible in doing the work without owning it — splitting RACI's overloaded R into doer vs helper. RACI-VS is notable for adding V = Verifier (checks the deliverable against acceptance criteria) and S = Signatory (approves the verified result), pulling verification into the assignment matrix itself. CAIRO's O explicitly marks roles deliberately excluded from a work item.
form_elements: Same matrix skeleton as RACI (work-item rows x role columns, one A per row)
S (Support): assists the Responsible without owning completion — doer/helper split
V (Verifier): checks the deliverable against defined acceptance criteria; distinct from both R and A
S (Signatory): formally approves after verification
O (Omitted/out-of-the-loop): explicit exclusion marker
Q (Quality review): a named quality-check involvement
findings.fit_notes: Mostly context: the variant explosion is itself evidence of the base form's expressive gap, and the report should describe rather than adopt the zoo. Two letters have real resonance here. S (Support) matches the dispatched-subagent-assists pattern (a lead-architect dispatch supporting a router-owned reconciliation). V (Verifier) is the interesting one for a system whose thesis is construction-definitions-precede-checks: a Verifier column names, per artifact kind, the role that runs the derived checks (LLM judge, reviewer role), keeping judge separate from generator — which §3's Goodharting mitigations already require. If the PO-vs-Architect matrix is built, RASCI-with-V (i.e., R/A/S/C/I plus a Verifier column) is a defensible shop dialect, provided each added letter carries a Deming-style operational definition rather than a vibe.

findings.name: Decision-rights matrices: RAPID (Bain) and DACI (Intuit/Atlassian)
findings.citation: RAPID: Rogers, P. & Blenko, M., "Who Has the D?: How Clear Decision Roles Enhance Organizational Performance", Harvard Business Review 84(1), January 2006 (hbr.org/2006/01/who-has-the-d-how-clear-decision-roles-enhance-organizational-performance; also bain.com/insights/who-has-the-d/) — Recommend / Agree / Perform / Input / Decide, exactly one Decider; identifies four recurring decision-bottleneck loci (global vs local, center vs business unit, function vs function, inside vs outside partners). DACI: Atlassian Team Playbook, "DACI: A Decision-Making Framework" (atlassian.com/team-playbook/plays/daci) — Driver / Approver / Contributors / Informed, one Approver; origin commonly attributed to Intuit in the 1980s (secondary attribution only, not primary-verified).
findings.what_it_defines: The decision-rights fork of the responsibility matrix: the unit of assignment is a DECISION, not a task or deliverable. RAPID assigns five roles per decision — Recommend (builds the proposal), Agree (must consent, a constrained veto), Input (consulted, voice not vote), Decide (the single D, commits the organization), Perform (executes once decided) — and was explicitly motivated by the failure mode RACI does not fix: task matrices leave decision authority ambiguous. DACI's contribution is splitting the two roles organizations systematically merge: the Driver (moves the decision process to a conclusion by an agreed date) vs the Approver (holds final authority). Both preserve the exactly-one-decider invariant.
form_elements: Unit of assignment: a named decision (not a task/deliverable)
Exactly one Decide/Approver per decision (the one-A rule at decision granularity)
Recommend/Driver as a distinct process-ownership role separate from authority
Agree: consent-required role with bounded veto (RAPID)
Input/Contributors: voice-not-vote consultation
Perform: execution role bound after the decision
Named bottleneck taxonomy for locating which decisions need explicit role assignment (RAPID)
findings.fit_notes: Directly relevant to the PO-vs-Architect investigation, because that question is partly decision-rights, not task assignment: who DECIDES scope vocabulary vs message-type selection vs decomposition is cleaner in RAPID terms than in RACI terms (the shop's discriminator rules are, in effect, an implicit D-assignment: PO holds the D on scope/vocabulary, Architect on vehicle/decomposition, the product authority on ratification). The Driver/Approver split maps to router-vs-authority: the router drives classification and dispatch to conclusion but never holds product authority — DACI names that separation precisely. Recommend describing both in §1.2's successor section and borrowing only the vocabulary: per-decision single-D assignments folded into role accountabilities, not a standalone RAPID chart. The Intuit origin claim for DACI must stay marked as unverified attribution if cited.

findings.name: Holacracy role format and governance amendment process
findings.citation: Holacracy Constitution v5.0, HolacracyOne (holacracy.org/constitution/5-0/; source text at github.com/holacracyone/Holacracy-Constitution, CC BY-SA 4.0): §1.1 role definition (name + Purpose + Domains + Accountabilities), §1.2/§1.4.1 role assignment and Role Lead, Article 5 governance process — §5.3.1 valid-proposal criteria (tension + concrete example + how the proposal reduces it), §5.3.2–5.3.3 objection-testing criteria, §5.4.5 integrative decision-making sequence. Book form: Robertson, B., Holacracy: The New Management System for a Rapidly Changing World, Henry Holt, 2015. Failure exemplar: Doyle, A., "Management and Organization at Medium", Medium blog, March 2016 (blog.medium.com/management-and-organization-at-medium-2228cc9d93e9) — Medium's exit after several years: coordination tax at scale, and "the act of codifying responsibilities in explicit detail hindered a proactive attitude and sense of communal ownership."
findings.what_it_defines: A constitutionalized role anatomy with strict role/person separation. A Role is a descriptive name plus three optional parts (§1.1): Purpose — "a capacity, potential, or goal that the Role will pursue or express"; Domains — "assets, processes, or other things the Role may exclusively control and regulate as its property"; Accountabilities — "ongoing activities the Role will manage and enact", by convention phrased as gerunds ("Implementing…", "Designing…"), a lintable authoring rule. People are not roles: a person filling a role is its Role Lead; Circle Leads assign roles (§1.4.1); one person may fill many roles and one role many people. Role definitions can be changed ONLY through the Governance Process (Article 5): a proposal must be grounded in a concrete Tension the proposer's role experienced (§5.3.1); it is processed through integrative decision-making (present → clarifying questions → reaction round → amend → objection round → integration, §5.4.5); objections must pass defined validity tests (§5.3.2) or the proposal stands. Governance outputs are recorded role amendments — an append/amend audit trail of the role set.
form_elements: Role = descriptive name + Purpose + Domains + Accountabilities (each part optional, all three typed)
Purpose: one-line pursued capacity/goal (why the role exists)
Domains: exclusive-control grants — property the role alone may regulate
Accountabilities: ongoing-activity list, gerund-phrased (verb-ing), not task scripts
Role/person separation: Role Lead assignment distinct from role definition; many-to-many
Amendment protocol: tension-grounded proposal + integrative decision-making + objection-validity tests; definition changes only via governance, recorded
Policies: named grants/constraints of authority attachable to domains
findings.fit_notes: The strongest external match found for this system's role layer. (a) Role/person separation maps exactly to definition-vs-instance: the .claude/agents file is the role, a dispatched subagent run is a Role Lead energizing it. (b) Domains are the missing formal name for the shop's exclusive bindings — RUP's one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule (§2.2) is precisely a Domain grant ("the PO exclusively controls features/ scenarios"), and phrasing artifact bindings as Domains would make the one-A property a structural feature of the role definition rather than a matrix-side rule. (c) Gerund accountability lists are near-isomorphic to the Scrum-style 4–8 accountability bullets §2.2 already recommends; Holacracy adds the enforceable phrasing convention. (d) The governance amendment protocol is an established, citable form for what the report elsewhere requires ad hoc — TOGAF's "stable but amendable under a change process" (§2.4) and the gated canonical-template promotion (§2.7): tension-grounded proposals with objection tests are a concrete protocol for amending role definitions under change control. Cautions: adopt the anatomy and amendment discipline, not the machinery (circles, elected facilitators, tactical meetings — heavy, human-meeting-shaped); and Medium's documented exit reason — exhaustive codification taxing proactivity — is a live risk for a system that compiles role text into agent context, arguing for Holacracy's own minimalism (all three role parts optional) plus the existing 200-line primer budget.

findings.name: Team Topologies team types and interaction modes
findings.citation: Skelton, M. & Pais, M., Team Topologies: Organizing Business and Technology Teams for Fast Flow, IT Revolution Press, 2019; concept definitions maintained at teamtopologies.com/key-concepts (wording verified): four team types — stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem, platform — and three interaction modes — collaboration ("working together for a defined period of time to discover new things"), X-as-a-Service ("one team provides and one team consumes something 'as a Service'"), facilitating ("one team helps and mentors another team").
findings.what_it_defines: Role-adjacent, not a role-definition format: it types TEAMS (not persons) into four kinds by their relationship to the flow of work, and — the transferable part — types the RELATIONSHIP between any two teams into exactly three interaction modes, each with defined semantics and an expected evolution (collaboration is deliberately time-bounded and should decay into X-as-a-Service as interfaces stabilize). The claim is that naming the interaction mode is itself an organizational design act: ambiguous inter-team relationships are a primary source of friction, and the three-mode vocabulary makes the intended relationship explicit and reviewable.
form_elements: Four team types: stream-aligned (owns a flow of change), enabling (helps stream-aligned teams overcome obstacles, detects missing capabilities), complicated-subsystem (deep-specialism component), platform (internal product accelerating stream-aligned teams)
Three interaction modes: collaboration (time-bounded joint discovery), X-as-a-Service (provider/consumer over a stable interface, minimal coordination), facilitating (one team mentors another)
Evolution rule: interaction modes are expected to shift over time (collaboration → X-as-a-Service) and the shift is a designed decision
Per-relationship declaration: each pair of teams names its current intended mode
findings.fit_notes: Included because it is the only verified established form that types role-to-role INTERACTION, a dimension absent from every format in the current §1.2 survey and from RACI (which types involvement in a deliverable, not the standing relationship between two roles). The mapping to this system is clean: lead-shop↔BC is X-as-a-Service by construction (the shop-msg contract, ADR-018's no-BC-source rule — the interface IS the service boundary); a clarify exchange is bounded collaboration; lead-architect answering BC clarifies verges on facilitating. Adoption should be limited to the interaction-mode triad as declared vocabulary — e.g., a role definition or primer names its intended mode per counterpart, making "the router does not collaborate with BCs, it consumes them as a service" a stated, checkable line rather than folklore. The four team types themselves are org-design for human teams and should stay descriptive context only.

checks.name: DITA 1.3 information typing and maps
checks.corrections: Source exists and most claims verify exactly: the linked information-typing page contains 'keep documentation focused and modular', names concept/task/reference as the core triad, cites Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique, and lists avoiding mixed content types as a stated benefit; the DITA-maps arch page contains the quoted 'organize topics and other resources into structured collections' and the hierarchy/relationships and key-definition/resolution claims; Errata 02 was approved 29 June 2018. Two substantive errors: (1) 'extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting' is wrong for glossaryEntry — the glossary entry (glossentry) topic type was introduced in DITA 1.1 (OASIS Standard, Aug 2007) and enhanced in 1.2; only the troubleshooting topic type is new in 1.3. (2) The root-element rule is incomplete: DITA 1.3 permits three roots — <topic> or a specialization, <map> or a specialization, OR the (unspecializable) <dita> element for multi-topic documents. Minor citation inconsistency: the text says 'Part 3 architectural spec' but the URL points to Part 2 (Technical Content Edition); the same arch-spec sections appear in both parts, and the linked information-typing page itself does not mention glossaryEntry/troubleshooting (those are covered in the tech-content document-types section).

checks.corrections: All claims verified. result.area_summary: The quality-management lineage fills the governance gap in the existing report: it is the one surveyed tradition whose core artifact is the controlled definition itself. Three contributions stand out. (1) ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5 plus the ISO 9000:2015 vocabulary supply the established form for governing versioned definition surfaces — the controlled-document regime (identification, format, review-and-approval, version control, availability-at-point-of-use, obsolete-document prevention, external-origin control) and the load-bearing maintain-vs-retain distinction between living definitions and immutable records. (2) The Shewhart(1939)→Deming-wheel(1950)→PDCA(1951/Ishikawa 1985)→PDSA(1986–1993)/Model-for-Improvement lineage supplies the improvement-loop FORM, with two structural facts the shop needs: Shewhart's circle is the original statement that specification precedes production precedes inspection and that inspection feeds re-specification; and the loop's terminal phase (PDCA Act, DMAIC Control) is defined as a document-control action — standardize the change into the governed surface — so improvement loops close in ratified-definition revisions, not ad-hoc fixes. PDSA's prediction-then-Study discipline is the established form for the judge-calibration loop the report already requires (EvalGen). (3) Six Sigma's CTQ tree is the strongest external analogue to derive-checks-from-ratified-definitions found in any tradition surveyed: a traceability tree from qualitative customer need through quality drivers to measurable requirements with pass criteria, converging exactly with Deming's operational definition already adopted in report §2.5(a); DMAIC contributes the phase-gate form where gates check deliverables (not activity) and are reviewed by an authority seat distinct from the performer. All phase names, page numbers, and clause facts below were verified against the cited sources this session (the Moen PDSA history paper was retrieved in full; paywalled ISO clause detail was cross-verified via the official ISO/TC 176 public guidance and multiple consistent secondary sources, noted per finding).

findings.name: ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5 — documented information (controlled-document regime)
findings.citation: ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems — Requirements, clause 7.5 (iso.org/standard/62085.html). Official public companion: ISO/TC 176/SC2/N1286, Guidance on the requirements for Documented Information of ISO 9001:2015 (iso.org/iso/documented_information.pdf). Clause detail cross-verified via N1286 and consistent secondary sources; the standard text itself is paywalled.
findings.what_it_defines: The requirements regime for controlled documents. 7.5.1: the QMS includes documented information required by the standard PLUS whatever the organization determines necessary for effectiveness (extent proportional to organization size, process complexity, competence). 7.5.2 (creating and updating): ensure (a) identification and description (e.g. title, date, author, reference number), (b) format (e.g. language, software version, graphics) and media (paper, electronic), (c) review and approval for suitability and adequacy. 7.5.3 (control): information must be available and suitable for use where and when needed, and adequately protected (loss of confidentiality, improper use, loss of integrity); control activities as applicable: distribution/access/retrieval/use; storage and preservation including legibility; control of changes (e.g. version control); retention and disposition. Documented information of external origin determined necessary must be identified and controlled; information retained as evidence of conformity must be protected from unintended alteration. The 2015 edition merged 'documents' and 'records' into one concept, 'documented information', with two verbs carrying the old distinction: MAINTAIN (keep current — definitional documents) vs RETAIN (keep as evidence — records).
form_elements: Two-tier scope rule: standard-required information + organization-determined-necessary information, extent proportional to complexity
Creation/update triple: identification-and-description, format-and-media, review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy
Availability rule: relevant version available at point of use, when needed
Obsolete-document rule: prevent unintended use of superseded versions
Change control: changes identified, current revision status known (version control named explicitly)
Control-activity checklist: distribution, access (view-only vs view-and-change), retrieval and use, storage and preservation, retention and disposition
External-origin documents identified and brought under control
Evidence records protected from unintended alteration
maintain (keep current) vs retain (keep as evidence) verb distinction
findings.fit_notes: Direct model for governing versioned prompt/skill/definition surfaces. The mapping is one-to-one: the definition corpus is 'documented information determined necessary'; ratification = review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy; the compiled-context assembly guarantee = relevant-version-available-at-point-of-use; the stale-compiled-prompt hazard = the obsolete-document rule; git + pinning (report §2.7, Langfuse algebra) = change control and revision status; canonical templates from shopsystem-templates = external-origin control; protection-from-unintended-alteration = the immutability rule for ADRs/session records. What ISO adds over what the report already has is the requirements CHECKLIST form — clause 7.5 is itself a derivable audit rubric for the governance layer, and audit traceability (which version was in force when a given artifact was produced) is exactly the judge-model/prompt-version pinning requirement of §2.6/§3. ADAPT: take the requirement checklist and the maintain/retain distinction; drop certification machinery, and let git supply the mechanics ISO leaves to procedure.

findings.name: ISO 9000:2015 vocabulary (documented information, record, verification/validation term system)
findings.citation: ISO 9000:2015, Quality management systems — Fundamentals and vocabulary, 4th ed., September 2015, clause 3 (iso.org/standard/45481.html; full text publicly readable on the ISO Online Browsing Platform). Term numbers 3.8.5/3.8.6/3.8.10 verified this session; other terms cited by name.
findings.what_it_defines: The controlled term system beneath document control and checking: document = 'information and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.5); documented information = 'information required to be controlled and maintained by an organization and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.6); record = 'document stating results achieved or providing evidence of activities performed' (3.8.10); specification = a document stating requirements; plus the linked cluster: requirement (need or expectation that is stated, generally implied or obligatory), conformity/nonconformity (fulfilment / non-fulfilment of a requirement), objective evidence, verification (confirmation via objective evidence that SPECIFIED REQUIREMENTS are fulfilled) vs validation (confirmation via objective evidence that requirements for a SPECIFIC INTENDED USE are fulfilled). Definitions are themselves written in a controlled defined-term-references-defined-term style.
form_elements: document / documented information / record as distinct defined terms
record defined by function: states results achieved or evidences activities performed
specification = document stating requirements
conformity = fulfilment of a requirement (the semantic of every check verdict)
verification vs validation split: against stated requirements vs against intended use
objective evidence as the admissibility condition for both
vocabulary itself maintained as a controlled, cross-referenced term system
findings.fit_notes: ADOPT as citable vocabulary anchors. Three distinctions do real work for the shop: (1) maintained-definition vs retained-record formalizes the split the report already draws in §2.4 (principles amended under change control vs ADRs immutable and superseded) and generalizes it to every artifact kind; (2) verification vs validation maps precisely onto mechanical-checks-against-the-definition vs fitness-judgment-against-intended-use (the §2.6 judged fitness tests are validation, the derived lint/schema checks are verification — naming this prevents category errors in check design); (3) conformity-as-fulfilment-of-a-requirement plus the objective-evidence condition restates the report's Deming operational-definition rule (§2.5a) in standards language. Costs nothing to adopt; the terms are stable, public, and already implicit in the system.

findings.name: ISO 10013:2021 — Guidance for documented information
findings.citation: ISO 10013:2021, Quality management systems — Guidance for documented information, 1st ed., March 2021, 14 pp. (iso.org/standard/75736.html; replaces ISO/TR 10013:2001). Existence, edition, committee, and scope verified; full text paywalled.
findings.what_it_defines: The how-to companion to 9001 clause 7.5: guidance on developing and maintaining the documented information a QMS needs, tailored to the organization — the traditional documentation hierarchy (policy / manual at the top, procedures, work instructions, forms and records at the bottom: altitude decreasing, specificity increasing), plus creation, revision-control, and distribution practice, updated in 2021 for digitized documentation and automated process-flow control.
form_elements: Documentation hierarchy: policy → procedure → work instruction → form/record (decreasing altitude, increasing specificity)
Guidance-not-requirements posture: one authoritative requirements clause (9001 7.5) with a separate non-binding practice guide
Tailoring rule: documentation extent fits the organization, not a fixed template
findings.fit_notes: CONTEXT-ONLY. The hierarchy idea (principle → process definition → skill body → record) parallels structures the report already anchors better elsewhere (15289 for artifact schemas, Agent Skills for the operational layer), and the 14-page guidance adds little beyond clause 7.5 itself. Its one citable structural lesson is the normative/informative split at the standards-architecture level: requirements live in one controlled place (9001 7.5) and practice guidance is a separate, subordinate, non-binding document — the same WCAG-style split the report adopts in §2.5(f). Cite it to show the document-control tradition itself observes construction-definition-precedes-guidance; do not adopt its content.

findings.name: Shewhart cycle (specification–production–inspection, 1939)
findings.tradition: Statistical quality control (Bell Labs / USDA Graduate School)
findings.citation: Shewhart, W. A., Statistical Method from the Viewpoint of Quality Control, The Graduate School, U.S. Department of Agriculture, 1939 (Dover reprint 1986), p. 45; edited by W. Edwards Deming. Quotation and page verified via Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle', Associates in Process Improvement (deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The original improvement-loop form. Shewhart takes the three mass-production steps — specification, production, inspection — and rules: 'These three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line... specification, production, and inspection correspond respectively to making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment, and testing the hypothesis. The three steps constitute a dynamic scientific process of acquiring knowledge.' Each phase is epistemically typed (hypothesis / experiment / test), and inspection's output is not a verdict alone but input to re-specification.
form_elements: Three phases: specification (hypothesis), production (experiment), inspection (test)
Ordering rule: specification precedes production precedes inspection
Circularity rule: inspection feeds re-specification; the line becomes a loop
Epistemic typing: each phase identified with a scientific-method step, making the loop a knowledge-acquisition process
findings.fit_notes: This is the primary-source ancestor of the shop's re-founding commitment: construction-definitions-precede-checks IS Shewhart's ordering (specification precedes inspection; inspection is meaningful only against a specification), and his circularity rule adds the closure the report currently leaves implicit — check results must be able to revise the ratified definition, under change control, or the loop is broken. ADAPT as a citable foundational principle plus one structural requirement: every derived check traces back to a specification clause, and every check outcome has a defined path back into specification revision. Not a process container (that role stays with 24774/ETVX per §2.1); it is the warrant beneath them.

findings.name: Deming wheel (1950) → Japanese PDCA (1951; Ishikawa 1985) — Act-as-standardization improvement loop
findings.citation: Deming, W. E., Elementary Principles of the Statistical Control of Quality, JUSE, 1950 (the eight-day JUSE seminar wheel: design with tests → make/test → sell → test in service through market research → redesign); Imai, M., Kaizen: The Key to Japan's Competitive Success, Random House, 1986, p. 60 (Japanese executives' recasting of the wheel as Plan–Do–Check–Act); Ishikawa, K., What Is Total Quality Control? The Japanese Way, Prentice-Hall, 1985, pp. 56–61 (PDCA subdivided: goals+methods, training+implementation, check effects, act). All as documented in Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle' (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The PDCA form and, critically, where each phase's outputs live. Plan: definition of the problem, goals and targets, and the METHODS for reaching them (Ishikawa; traceable to Mizuno 1959) — the plan phase's output is itself a standard-to-be. Do: education/training plus implementation. Check: evaluation of results against the plan. Act: 'back to plan if the results are unsatisfactory, or STANDARDIZATION if the results are satisfactory' — PDCA 'emphasized the prevention of error recurrence by establishing standards and the ongoing modification of those standards' (Moen), with Ishikawa adding that good control means standards revised constantly to reflect consumer voices and next-process requirements. In Japanese practice each loop turn is documented in the QC-story format alongside the seven basic tools (Lillrank & Kano 1989, per Moen).
form_elements: Four phases: Plan (problem, goals, methods) / Do (train, implement) / Check (evaluate) / Act (standardize or re-plan)
Terminal-phase rule: a successful loop turn ENDS in a document-control action — the change is written into the standard
Failure path defined: unsatisfactory results loop back to Plan, not to ad-hoc patching
Standards are living: revised continuously from downstream voices (consumer complaints, next process)
QC story as the per-turn documented record of the loop
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT as the shape of the shop's improvement loop over its definition surfaces. The load-bearing element is Act-as-standardization: a finding from any check or reconciliation is not closed until the governed surface (definition, skill, prompt, fitness set) is revised and re-ratified — or the finding is explicitly sent back to Plan. This gives the report's Fagan-style checklist-item add/retire rule (§2.5d) and criteria-drift calibration loop (§3) their missing outer loop and names its termination condition. The QC-story precedent maps to the existing session-record/finding artifact kinds: one documented record per loop turn. Drop the statistical seven-tools apparatus; keep the loop skeleton, the two exit paths, and the standards-are-living rule (which matches TOGAF's Stable-but-amendable, already adopted in §2.4).

findings.name: Deming PDSA (1986/1993) and the Model for Improvement (prediction-driven learning loop)
findings.tradition: Deming; Associates in Process Improvement / IHI improvement science
findings.citation: Deming, W. E., Out of the Crisis, MIT Press, 1986, p. 88 (Shewhart cycle reintroduced); Deming, W. E., The New Economics, MIT Press, 1993, p. 135 ('Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement — the PDSA Cycle'; Deming to Moen, 17 Nov 1990: 'be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA'); Moen, Nolan, Provost, Improving Quality Through Planned Experimentation, McGraw-Hill, 1991, p. 11 (prediction added to Plan); Langley, Nolan, Nolan, 'The Foundation of Improvement', Quality Progress, June 1994, p. 81; Langley et al., The Improvement Guide, 2nd ed., Jossey-Bass, 2009, p. 24 (Model for Improvement). All verified via Moen's PDSA history paper (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The learning variant of the loop, distinct from PDCA by Deming's own insistence (he called PDCA unrelated to his cycle: 'They bear no relation to each other', GAO roundtable 1980). Plan: plan a change or test aimed at improvement, INCLUDING a stated prediction and the theory behind it (Moen/Nolan/Provost 1991). Do: carry it out, preferably small scale. Study (not Check — 'check' means 'to hold back'): compare observed results against the prediction — the deductive/inductive interplay that produces learning. Act: adopt, abandon, or run the cycle again under different conditions. The Model for Improvement (1994) frames every cycle with three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know that a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement? Moen's summary of the division of labor: PDCA is used for implementation and compliance; PDSA for testing and implementing (learning).
form_elements: Plan requires a written prediction plus its theory, before execution
Do is deliberately small-scale (pilot before adoption)
Study compares observed against predicted — not merely 'did it work'
Act has three defined outcomes: adopt / abandon / re-run under changed conditions
Three framing questions, the second being an explicit check-derivation question ('How will we know that a change is an improvement?')
Two distinct loops for two jobs: PDSA for testing/learning, PDCA for standardization/compliance
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT, with a precise assignment: the shop needs BOTH loops, and this lineage names the difference. PDCA (previous finding) governs standardization of ratified definitions; PDSA is the established form for the judge-calibration and criteria-drift loop the report already requires (§2.6, §3: EvalGen's iterative human-calibration loop IS a PDSA cycle once named). Concretely: a fitness-set or judge-prompt revision should record a prediction (which verdicts will change and why) before deployment, and its Study step compares sampled product-authority grading against that prediction — turning open question 7 (calibration governance) from an ownership question into a form with defined phase outputs. Question 2 of the Model for Improvement is a one-line warrant for the whole re-founding: no change without a stated way of knowing, i.e. no definition without derivable checks.

findings.name: CTQ (critical-to-quality) tree — need → driver → measurable requirement derivation
findings.tradition: Six Sigma (Motorola/GE lineage); ancestor in QFD
findings.citation: ASQ Quality Glossary, 'critical to quality' (asq.org/quality-resources/quality-glossary): CTQs are the 'key measurable characteristics of a product or process whose performance standards or specification limits must be met in order to satisfy the customer'. Authoritative handbook treatment: Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (ISBN 9780873899413, aligned to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way: How GE, Motorola, and Other Top Companies Are Honing Their Performance, McGraw-Hill, 2000 (VOC-to-CTQ translation in GE-lineage practice). Matrix ancestor: Hauser & Clausing, 'The House of Quality', Harvard Business Review 66(3), May–June 1988, pp. 63–73 (hbr.org/1988/05/the-house-of-quality). No single primary inventor source exists for the tree itself — it is GE-era practice; ASQ is the authoritative secondary anchor.
findings.what_it_defines: The canonical derivation from qualitative to checkable, as a three-level tree with traceability: (1) NEED — the customer's requirement in the customer's qualitative language; (2) DRIVERS — the quality characteristics by which the customer will judge whether the need is met; (3) CTQ PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS — for each driver, one or more measurable characteristics, each with a specification limit or target that operationalizes 'good enough'. The admissibility rule is that leaves must be measurable; the structural rule is that every leaf traces up through a driver to a stated need, and drilling stops when a requirement is concrete enough to measure against. QFD's House of Quality is the denser matrix ancestor: weighted customer attributes crossed with engineering characteristics carrying objective target values.
form_elements: Three fixed levels: qualitative need → quality drivers → measurable requirements
Leaf admissibility rule: a leaf is a measurable characteristic with a specification limit/target, or the derivation is unfinished
Full traceability: every check traces to a driver, every driver to a need
Coverage test in both directions: a need with no leaves is unmeasured; a leaf with no need is unauthorized
Derivation performed in the Define phase, i.e. before measurement or improvement work begins
findings.fit_notes: The strongest single-form analogue found in any tradition to the shop's derive-checks-from-ratified-definitions move. Mapping: ratified construction definition = need level; the definition's stated qualities/outcomes = drivers; each derived mechanical check or rubric item = a CTQ leaf, admissible only once operationalized — which is exactly Deming's operational definition already adopted in §2.5(a), and the concrete table form that open question 6 (outcome→indicator→rubric traceability ceremony) asks for. ADAPT: adopt the three-level derivation record and both coverage tests per artifact kind (a small need→driver→check table stored with the fitness set, giving 330xx-style traceability without assessor machinery); drop sigma-level targets and statistical capability apparatus, and treat rubric anchors (Ragas/Brookhart forms, §2.5b) as the specification-limit analogue for qualitative leaves.

findings.name: DMAIC — defined process with phase deliverables and tollgate reviews
findings.citation: ASQ, 'DMAIC Process: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control' (asq.org/quality-resources/dmaic); Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (organized to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge, which is itself structured by DMAIC phase); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way, McGraw-Hill, 2000. Tollgate vocabulary confirmed in ASQ practice materials (ASQ section greenbelt 'Define Tollgate' curriculum).
findings.what_it_defines: A data-driven improvement process for existing processes, defined as five phases each specified by its deliverables rather than its activities: Define (project charter, voice of customer and CTQs, high-level process map); Measure (baseline performance, operational definitions of the measures, measurement-system validation); Analyze (root causes identified and verified with data); Improve (solutions implemented and validated against the baseline); Control (control plan, standardized and documented process, monitoring installed, handoff to the process owner). Phase boundaries carry tollgate reviews: a formal checkpoint where an authority seat distinct from the team doing the work (sponsor/champion/Master Black Belt) reviews the phase deliverables for completeness and quality and formally authorizes entry to the next phase.
form_elements: Five named phases, each defined by exit deliverables, not activity lists
Tollgate/phase-gate: deliverable review at each boundary, pass required to proceed
Separation of seats: gate review is performed by an authority distinct from the performer
Measure phase institutionalizes operational definitions and measurement-system validation before any judgment of the process
Control phase termination rule: the effort is not complete until the change is standardized into controlled documentation with monitoring in place and ownership transferred
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT selectively; as a process container it mostly reinforces forms the report already chose (deliverable-defined phases ≈ 24774 outcomes plus ETVX exit criteria, §2.1). Three elements are independently adoptable: (1) the distinct-seat tollgate — gate review by an authority other than the producer — maps directly onto product-authority ratification of definitions and the lead/BC review split, and is the established name for that governance shape; (2) Measure-before-Analyze, with measurement-system validation, is the process-level form of judge calibration: validate the judge/check before trusting its verdicts about artifacts; (3) the Control-phase termination rule independently converges with PDCA's Act-as-standardization — in this whole lineage, improvement work terminates in a document-control action on a governed surface, which is precisely the closure rule the shop's quality layer should ratify. Do not adopt belt hierarchy, project-charter ceremony, or the statistical toolkit.

checks.name: RACI responsibility-assignment matrix (RAM)
checks.corrections: All load-bearing citations check out: Wikipedia RAM article exists, defines RACI, lists the variants, cites PMBOK 5th ed. p. 262, uses 'linear responsibility chart' as an alternate name, and carries no origin history (supporting the no-documented-originator claim). PMBOK 6th-ed RACI-chart glossary quote confirmed verbatim via PMP secondary literature — matching the finding's own hedge. Cleland & King, Systems Analysis and Project Management, McGraw-Hill 1968 confirmed. PMI library article at the exact URL confirmed (direct fetch 403s due to bot-blocking, but the page exists and discusses Cleland & King). One minor caveat: the RAM glossary wording 'a grid that shows the project resources assigned to each work package' was attributed by one secondary source to the 7th edition rather than the 6th; the wording is standard PMBOK glossary language but the edition pin rests on secondary quoting, as the finding itself discloses. Wikipedia's one-A phrasing ('according to some theories... only one accountable') supports the finding's careful claim that the one-A rule is practitioner doctrine, not PMBOK glossary text. checks.name: RASCI and the RACI letter-set variant family
checks.corrections: Wikipedia RAM article carries every claimed variant with matching letter expansions: RASCI/RACIS/RASIC/RASI (S=Support), RACIQ (Q=Quality review), RACIO/CAIRO (O=Omitted/Out-of-the-loop), RACI-VSL (V=Verifier, S=Signatory — the finding's 'RACI-VS(L)' rendering is consistent), PARIS (Participant/Accountable/Review required/Input required/Sign-off required), RACI+F (Facilitation, in Scrum projects). Two soft claims are interpretive rather than sourced: that every variant 'preserves the one-A rule' (the article does not state this per-variant) and that RASCI is 'the most adopted' (plausible practitioner consensus, uncited). Neither undermines the citation, which correctly frames the inventory as 'as carried on the Wikipedia RAM article' with no authoritative standard.

checks.name: Decision-rights matrices: RAPID (Bain) and DACI (Intuit/Atlassian)
checks.corrections: HBR January 2006 article by Paul Rogers and Marcia Blenko confirmed with exact title at the cited hbr.org URL (HBR 84(1) = Jan 2006 issue, correct). Bain's companion piece confirms the five RAPID roles verbatim, the exactly-one-Decider rule ('the single point of accountability'), and all four bottleneck loci word-for-word ('global versus local, center versus business unit, function versus function or inside versus outside partners'). The Intuit-1980s origin is indeed a widespread secondary attribution (LogRocket, ProductPlan, airfocus, etc.) absent from the Atlassian page and with no primary source — precisely as the finding marks it ('secondary attribution only, not primary-verified').

checks.name: Team Topologies team types and interaction modes

checks.name: DITA 1.3 information typing and maps
checks.corrections: Source exists and most quotes verify verbatim, but three corrections are needed. Also the 1.3 Technical Content edition defines a larger type set (concept, reference, strict task, general task, machinery task, troubleshooting, glossentry, glossgroup), so "closed base set plus glossaryEntry/troubleshooting" undersells it; and the cited information-typing page itself enumerates "concept, task, reference, or learningContent" and never mentions glossaryEntry or troubleshooting. (2) The normative root-element rule is incomplete as stated: per the spec a DITA document may also have <dita> as its root (an unspecializable container for multiple sibling topics), not only <topic>/<map>/a specialization of one. (3) The citation says "Part 3 architectural spec" but the URL points to Part 2 (tech-content edition); the same archSpec topics appear in both editions, so it is a mismatch, not a fabrication. Everything else checks out verbatim: "a practice designed to keep documentation focused and modular", "Avoid mixing content types, thereby losing reader focus", the Robert Horn Information Mapping + Hughes Aircraft STOP lineage sentence, "All topics have the same basic structure" with new types defined as specializations of <topic>, the maps quotes ("DITA maps are documents that organize topics and other resources into structured collections of information"; maps "specify hierarchy and the relationships among the topics; they also provide the contexts in which keys are defined and resolved"), OASIS Standard dated 17 December 2015, and Errata 02 approved 29 June 2018.

The 'Documentation hierarchy' form element should be re-attributed to the 2001 TR or reframed as optional/example in 2021. The digitization update claim is confirmed (new 'workflow'/'automated workflow' definition 3.3, clause 4.2.4.6, electronic-media notes). checks.name: Deming wheel (1950) → Japanese PDCA (1951; Ishikawa 1985) — Act-as-standardization improvement loop
checks.corrections: Fully verified against the Moen paper read in full. Deming 1950 'Elementary Principles of the Statistical Control of Quality', JUSE, and the wheel's steps (design with tests → make/test → sell → test in service through market research → redesign) match; Imai's recasting claim matches (Moen ref [6], Random House, p. 60 — note Moen's reference list has a typo dating it '1886'; 1986 is correct as the finding states); Ishikawa 1985 Prentice-Hall pp. 56–61 with goals+methods in Plan and training in Do matches ref [7]; the load-bearing quotes are verbatim in Moen: Act = 'back to plan if the results are unsatisfactory or standardization if the results are satisfactory', and 'emphasized the prevention of error recurrence by establishing standards and the ongoing modification of those standards'; Ishikawa on standards revised constantly for consumer voices and next-process requirements confirmed; Mizuno 1959 traceability confirmed; Lillrank & Kano 1989 (their book, pp. 23–25) with QC story + seven tools as kaizen foundation confirmed. 'Each loop turn is documented in the QC-story format' is a mild extrapolation of Moen's wording but faithful in substance.

checks.name: Deming PDSA (1986/1993) and the Model for Improvement (prediction-driven learning loop)
checks.corrections: Fully verified against the Moen paper: Out of the Crisis 1986 p. 88 (ref [10]); The New Economics 1993 p. 135 and the name 'Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement - the PDSA Cycle' (ref [11]); the 17 Nov 1990 letter to Moen with the verbatim 'be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA'; the GAO roundtable (19 Aug 1980) verbatim 'They bear no relation to each other'; Moen/Nolan/Provost 1991 p. 11 adding required prediction and theory to Plan, with Study comparing observed data to the prediction; Deming's warning that 'check' means 'to hold back'; Langley/Nolan/Nolan 'The Foundation of Improvement', Quality Progress, June 1994, p. 81 (ref [16]); The Improvement Guide 2nd ed., Jossey-Bass, 2009, p. 24 (ref [18]); and Moen's summary 'PDCA is used for implementation and compliance... PDSA is used for testing and implementing'. Minor caveat: the small-scale Do and the adopt/abandon/re-run Act outcomes sit in Deming's 1993 cycle figure (an image in the PDF, not extractable text) — they are standard, uncontroversial 1993-PDSA content but were not text-verified this session.
